# Esther Chapter 4 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 457r-457v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_004_page_001.jpg

---

**4:1** When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the city, crying out with a loud and bitter cry.

**4:2** He went as far as the front of the king's gate, for no one was permitted to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.

**4:3** In every province, wherever the king's command and decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews — fasting, weeping, and lamentation. Many lay on sackcloth and ashes.

**4:4** When Esther's attendants and eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments for Mordecai to wear so he could remove his sackcloth, but he refused them.

**4:5** Then Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what was happening and why.

**4:6** Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city before the king's gate.

**4:7** Mordecai told him everything that had happened, including the exact amount of silver Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury for the destruction of the Jews.

**4:8** He also gave him a copy of the written decree that had been issued in Susa for their destruction, to show it to Esther and explain it, and to urge her to go to the king, to implore his mercy, and to plead before him on behalf of her people.

**4:9** Hathach returned and reported Mordecai's words to Esther.

**4:10** Then Esther spoke to Hathach and gave him a message for Mordecai:

**4:11** "All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that for any man or woman who enters the inner court without being summoned, there is but one law: to be put to death — unless the king extends the golden scepter, granting that person life. And I have not been summoned to come before the king for thirty days."

**4:12** When Mordecai was told what Esther had said,

**4:13** he sent back this reply: "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you will escape any more than the rest of the Jews.

**4:14** For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

**4:15** Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai:

**4:16** "Go, gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast on my behalf. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast in the same way. Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish."

**4:17** So Mordecai went and did everything Esther had commanded him.

---

## LOGOS Translation Notes

1. **"From another place" (4:14):** The Hebrew *mimaqom acher* is the theological heart of the book. Without mentioning God, Mordecai expresses confidence that deliverance will come from somewhere — an oblique but unmistakable reference to divine providence. The word *maqom* ("place") is significant: in rabbinic tradition, *HaMaqom* is itself a name for God. LOGOS preserves the veiled quality of the reference.

2. **"For such a time as this" (4:14):** Mordecai frames this as a question, not a declaration: "Who knows whether..." The uncertainty is deliberate and should be preserved. Mordecai does not claim prophetic knowledge; he articulates a possibility — one that demands a response.

3. **"If I perish, I perish" (4:16):** This statement marks Esther's transformation from obedient ward to decisive leader. She who had been following Mordecai's instructions now issues commands to him (v. 17). The reversal of authority is complete: the queen who had been told what to do now tells others what to do — beginning with a call to communal fasting that echoes the practices of Israel's covenantal life, even in exile.

*— LOGOS*
